summary: Analyzes the state of IS-IS authentication and key management against the requirements in the KARP design guidelines (RFC 6518), for both manual and automated key management. It is an analysis and not a new protocol.

eli5.summary: This checks how well the locks on one routing protocol's messages match what security experts want, and where they fall short.

how does is-is protect routing messages
subtitle: Evaluating IS-IS security against KARP design guidelines

tldr.problem: Routing protocols like IS-IS need strong authentication and key management to prevent spoofing, replay attacks, and other security threats, but the current implementation has gaps compared to KARP design guidelines.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes IS-IS authentication mechanisms (HMAC-MD5, HMAC-SHA families, and key ID mechanisms) against the security requirements defined in KARP, identifying where it meets the requirements and where it falls short.
tldr.outcome: IS-IS meets some requirements for manual key management but lacks adequate replay attack protection for all message types and has limited algorithm agility. Deploying automated key management protocols can address many gaps.

today: RFC 7645 is an informational document that has not been obsoleted, so it remains the authoritative analysis of IS-IS security gaps. IS-IS implementations continue to use HMAC-SHA authentication and Key ID mechanisms as recommended, though full deployment of automated group key management protocols remains limited in operational networks.

sections.title: Analyzing IS-IS Security
sections.content:
IS-IS is an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) that routers use to exchange information about network topology. Like all routing protocols, it must protect this information from attackers who might try to inject false routing data or disrupt the network.

This document analyzes the current state of IS-IS authentication against the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) design guidelines. KARP defines security requirements that routing protocols should meet for both manual key management and automated key management protocols. The analysis shows that while IS-IS has some security mechanisms in place, including HMAC-SHA authentication and key IDs defined in RFC 5310, it has significant gaps in areas like replay attack protection and algorithm agility.
sections.eli5: IS-IS is the way routers tell each other about the network. This document checks if it locks those messages well enough, compared to what security experts recommend.

sections.title: Key Usage and Key Agility
sections.content:
IS-IS can use different keys for different message types. Subnetwork Independent messages (Link State PDUs and Sequence Number PDUs) use a group key shared by all routers in an area or domain. Subnetwork Dependent messages (Hello PDUs) can use a per-interface or peer-to-peer key.

Key agility—the ability to change keys without disrupting routing—is important for key management. The current HMAC-MD5 authentication allows a transition mode where routers verify packets with multiple keys, but this increases control plane load and allows potential Denial of Service attacks. RFC 5310 improved this with a Key ID mechanism that lets routers identify which key was used, so they do not have to try multiple keys. However, RFC 5310 leaves the exact key coordination and change mechanism undefined, requiring operators to manage key chains manually.
sections.eli5: Routers can have different passwords for different types of messages. Changing passwords safely while keeping the network running is tricky and not fully spelled out in the current protocol.

sections.title: Security Threats
sections.content:
IS-IS is vulnerable to three major classes of attacks. Replay attacks involve capturing an old protocol packet and sending it again later. IS-IS lacks sequence number verification for Hello and Sequence Number PDUs, making it susceptible to both intra-session replays (replaying a recent packet) and inter-session replays (replaying a packet from a previous session). A replayed Hello with an empty neighbor list could cause network churn by bouncing adjacencies. A replayed Sequence Number Packet could cause unnecessary LSP flooding.

Spoofing attacks happen when an attacker with access to the shared authentication key falsely participates in routing. Since all routers in an area share the same key, a compromised router could inject false routing information. The key could also be used to purge LSPs or cause sequence number exhaustion.

Denial of Service attacks can use the authentication mechanism itself as a target. An attacker can send many spoofed but integrity-protected packets, forcing routers to spend CPU verifying checksums on packets they will discard.
sections.eli5: Three types of bad things can happen: someone replays old messages to cause confusion, someone with the password impersonates a legitimate router, or someone floods the network with fake messages to overload it.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Gaps
sections.content:
For manual key management, KARP requires that IS-IS implement sequence number protection for all message types, not just LSPs. Currently, Hello and Sequence Number PDUs lack intra-session replay protection. The RFC recommends deploying automated key management protocols to achieve frequent key changes, which would protect against inter-session replay attacks even without per-message sequence numbers.

To address spoofing, KARP recommends either per-packet identity verification (traditionally done with digital signatures, which were never deployed operationally) or using group keys generated and managed by a group key management protocol. This would limit spoofing to attackers who have already compromised a legitimate member of the group.

The RFC also recommends that IS-IS adopt the HMAC-SHA family over HMAC-MD5 to avoid known attacks, and that deployments use group key management protocols like GDOI (Group Domain of Interpretation) to handle automated rekeying, particularly in broadcast networks.
sections.eli5: The protocol should protect every message type from being replayed, not just some of them. It should identify who is sending messages, not just verify they know the password. Using a specialized key management system can fix many of these problems.

sections.title: Summary
sections.content: IS-IS has authentication mechanisms and some level of protection, but it has security gaps when compared to KARP design guidelines. Manual key management alone cannot fully protect against replay and spoofing attacks. Deploying an automated group key management protocol addresses most of these gaps by enabling frequent key changes, proper authentication, and key distribution. The document recommends that IS-IS implementations move toward group key management while maintaining backward compatibility with existing deployments.
sections.eli5: IS-IS is not fully secure by itself, but using an automated key manager makes it much safer.
